title: 2. What the Company Does: Segments, Revenue Mix & Concrete Examples

epigraph.quote: Six distinct economic engines—from 4%-margin warehouse clubs to 62%-margin nicotine franchises—coexist inside one ticker.
epigraph.author: XLP Sub-Industry Disaggregation

web_blocks.text: 2.1 Six GICS Sub-Industries and Top-Heavy Concentration Inside XLP

web_blocks.html: Unlike a single operating company, XLP is a curated basket of six distinct consumer staples sub-industries. As of November 19, 2026, its weights break down cleanly: Consumer Staples Distribution & Retail (34.75%), Beverages (19.76%), Household Products (18.43%), Food Products (15.20%), Tobacco (10.39%), and Personal Care Products (1.47%). Its top 10 holdings make up 64.28% of the fund, so ten mega-caps drive nearly two-thirds of XLP's cash flows. The remaining 24 holdings—including Kroger, Sysco, Kimberly-Clark, General Mills, Hershey, Monster Beverage, Keurig Dr Pepper, Clorox, Church & Dwight, and Estée Lauder—share the other 35.72%.

web_blocks.text: 2.2 Concrete Real-World Walkthroughs of Each Economic Engine

web_blocks.html: 1. Distribution & Retail (34.75% — Walmart, Costco, Target, Kroger, Sysco, Dollar General, Dollar Tree): Picture a family in Ohio ordering $180 of weekly groceries on Walmart's app for two-hour pickup. Or picture a shopper swiping a Costco Executive card at one of 914 warehouses for Kirkland Signature olive oil and rotisserie chicken. XLP captures both checkouts. Walmart generated $713.2 billion in FY26 total revenue across 10,900+ stores and 280 million weekly visits. It also layered on $6.75B in membership and other income plus a $6.4 billion global ad business (Walmart Connect grew 41% ex-VIZIO in Q4 FY26). Costco runs an even purer fee model. In FY25, it earned $269.91 billion in net sales at thin markups, while collecting $5.32 billion in membership fees—over half of its $10.38 billion operating income. Target adds $106.57 billion in sales, anchored by $23.8B in Food & Beverage, $18.6B in Household Essentials, and its Roundel ad arm.

2. Beverages (19.76% — Coca-Cola, PepsiCo, Keurig Dr Pepper, Monster Beverage, Constellation Brands, Brown-Forman): Consider a 12-pack of Coca-Cola Zero Sugar, which grew unit case volume 14% globally in FY25. Under Coca-Cola's asset-light concentrate model, KO sells proprietary syrup to independent bottlers. Those bottlers handle the capital-heavy trucks, bottling lines, and store coolers. That setup enabled KO to post a 31.2% comparable operating margin on $47.9 billion in FY25 net revenues. PepsiCo pairs company-owned North American bottling with its Frito-Lay snack powerhouse. In FY25, PepsiCo Foods North America (PFNA) generated $27.53 billion of PepsiCo's $93.93 billion net revenue and $6.17 billion of its $11.50 billion GAAP operating profit.

3. Household & Personal Care Products (19.90% combined — P&G, Colgate-Palmolive, Kimberly-Clark, Clorox, Church & Dwight, Estée Lauder, Kenvue): Every morning, billions of consumers brush with Crest or Colgate, shave with Gillette, wash clothes with Tide, and feed pets Hill's Science Diet. Procter & Gamble posted $87.03 billion in FY26 net sales across five units: Fabric & Home Care ($30.31B), Baby, Feminine & Family Care ($20.40B), Beauty ($16.02B), Health Care ($12.46B), and Grooming ($6.92B). P&G earned a 50.2% gross margin and 22.7% operating margin. Colgate-Palmolive commands 60.1% gross margins on $20.38 billion of FY25 sales, with two-thirds of revenue generated outside the United States.

4. Food Products (15.20% — Mondelez, Kraft Heinz, General Mills, Hershey, Tyson Foods, Kellanova, ADM): This sleeve owns center-of-store pantry staples, snacks, and protein processing, from Oreo cookies and Cadbury chocolate to Cheerios and Reese's. Mondelez generated $38.54 billion in FY25 net revenues across 150+ countries ($15.03B Europe, $10.68B North America, $7.93B AMEA, $4.90B Latin America). However, record cocoa inflation cut its reported gross margin by 1,070 bps to 28.4%. 5. Tobacco (10.39% — Philip Morris International, Altria): Two rival nicotine strategies sit side by side. PMI is shifting aggressively into smoke-free products—IQOS heated tobacco and ZYN oral pouches—which reached $16.9 billion (41.5% of PMI's $40.6B FY25 net revenues) across 106 markets. Altria defends a shrinking U.S. cigarette base (Marlboro volume down 12.2% in FY25) with 62.4% adjusted OCI margins and $7.0 billion in annual dividends.

web_blocks.text: 2.3 Beyond the Top 10: The Remaining 24 Constituents & Sub-Industry Economics

web_blocks.html: While the top 10 names command 64.28% of XLP, the other 24 constituents provide vital breadth. In Distribution & Retail, Kroger runs traditional supermarkets, Sysco supplies restaurants and hospitals, and Dollar General and Dollar Tree serve rural fill-in trips. In Beverages, Monster Beverage and Keurig Dr Pepper add energy drinks and coffee, while Constellation Brands and Brown-Forman add beer and spirits. In Household & Personal Care, Kimberly-Clark, Clorox, Church & Dwight, Estée Lauder, and Kenvue cover paper, bleach, and skincare. In Food Products, General Mills, Hershey, Kraft Heinz, Tyson, Kellanova, Campbell's, Conagra, J.M. Smucker, McCormick, and ADM anchor packaged meals and ingredients.

web_blocks.takeaway: Sub-segment disaggregation shows profit pools are even more concentrated than revenue: Frito-Lay (PFNA) drives over half of PepsiCo's GAAP profit, and Walmart U.S. drives 84% of Walmart's operating income.

web_blocks.html: Geographic Revenue Footprint: Every company in XLP is domiciled in the United States, yet the fund's underlying revenue is deeply global. Coca-Cola, Colgate-Palmolive (~67% ex-U.S.), Mondelez ($27.86B ex-North America), and Philip Morris International earn most of their cash abroad. By contrast, Walmart U.S. ($483.0B), Sam's Club ($93.0B), Target ($106.57B), Kroger, and Altria ($20.14B net-of-excise) anchor XLP in U.S. household spending.

Dividend & Cash-Distribution Mechanics: XLP collects dividends from all 34 holdings and pays out net investment income every quarter in March, June, September, and December. After deducting its 0.08% fee, XLP delivers a 2.35% 30-Day SEC Yield and a 2.44% trailing distribution yield. That tracks very closely to the underlying index's 2.46% dividend yield.

book_paragraphs: To understand what XLP actually owns, forget the abstract label 'Consumer Staples' for a moment. Picture a typical Saturday morning errand run. You drive to Costco, flash your membership card, and load a cart with Kirkland Signature paper towels, rotisserie chicken, and sparkling water. On the way home, you stop at Walmart for Tide Pods, Crest toothpaste, and a twelve-pack of Coca-Cola Zero Sugar. At checkout, you grab Oreo cookies or a can of ZYN pouches. Every item in that trip—and the cash registers you paid at—sits inside XLP.

When we open up XLP's 34 holdings, we find six distinct GICS sub-industries running on very different engines. The largest sleeve, at 34.75% of the fund, is Consumer Staples Distribution & Retail. It is anchored by Walmart at 11.37%, Costco at 9.82%, and Target at 4.34%, alongside Kroger and Sysco. These are massive, low-margin, high-turn logistics machines. Walmart moved $713.2 billion of goods in fiscal 2026 across 10,900+ stores, earning just over four cents of operating profit per sales dollar.

Costco's merchandise markup is even thinner, yet it collected $5.32 billion in pure-margin membership fees in fiscal 2025. Those fees made up over half of its $10.38 billion operating income. Meanwhile, Walmart layered a $6.4 billion digital ad business on top of its 280 million weekly customer visits.

Move from the retailer to the shelf, and margins jump sharply. Beverages make up 19.76% of XLP, led by Coca-Cola at 7.53% and PepsiCo at 4.15%. Coca-Cola sells proprietary syrup concentrates to independent bottlers worldwide. Because bottlers fund the trucks and bottling lines, Coca-Cola earned a 31.2% comparable operating margin on $47.9 billion in 2025 revenue. PepsiCo pairs North American bottling with Frito-Lay snacks, which generated $6.17 billion of PepsiCo's $11.50 billion GAAP operating profit.

Next come Household Products at 18.43% and Personal Care at 1.47%, led by Procter & Gamble at 7.90% and Colgate-Palmolive at 4.50%. P&G is an $87.0 billion consumer science engine spanning Tide, Pampers, Gillette, Crest, and Bounty. It posted a 50.2% gross margin and 22.7% operating margin in fiscal 2026. Colgate-Palmolive converts its oral-care lead and Hill's Pet Nutrition business into a 60.1% gross margin on $20.38 billion of sales.

The final two sleeves carry the sharpest cross-currents in the ETF. Food Products represent 15.20% of XLP, led by Mondelez at 4.30% alongside General Mills, Hershey, and Kraft Heinz. These firms are battling cocoa cost spikes and shifting diets. Tobacco makes up 10.39% through Philip Morris International (5.88%) and Altria (4.49%). PMI has shifted 41.5% of its $40.6 billion revenue into smoke-free IQOS and ZYN. Altria, meanwhile, is managing a 10% drop in domestic cigarette volumes while harvesting 62.4% adjusted operating margins to fund a $7.0 billion dividend.

Beyond the top ten giants that command 64.28% of XLP, the other twenty-four holdings round out the household budget. Kroger runs regional supermarkets, Sysco supplies restaurant kitchens, and Dollar General serves rural fill-in trips. Monster Beverage and Keurig Dr Pepper add energy drinks and coffee, while Kimberly-Clark, Clorox, and Church & Dwight cover paper and cleaning. When families eat out less, Sysco slows down while Kroger and General Mills pick up the slack.

Let us also look one level deeper inside the flagship companies. At Walmart, the U.S. division generated $483.0 billion in sales and $25.16 billion in operating income—about 84% of consolidated operating profit. At P&G, Fabric & Home Care alone produced $30.31 billion in sales and $7.29 billion in pre-tax profit. At PepsiCo, snacks generated over half of GAAP operating profit despite trailing beverages slightly in revenue.

Geographically, XLP blends domestic retail with global brands. Coca-Cola, Colgate-Palmolive, and Mondelez earn roughly two-thirds of their sales outside the United States. Walmart, Target, Kroger, and Altria remain heavily U.S.-focused. That mix cushions XLP against single-country slowdowns while exposing its CPG sleeve to currency swings.

Every quarter—in March, June, September, and December—XLP sweeps up cash dividends from all thirty-four holdings. It deducts its 0.08% fee and passes the net cash to shareholders, yielding 2.44% trailing. Keep this full architecture in mind as we follow the dollars into Chapter 3: XLP is a self-rebalancing wrapper across the entire consumer-essentials value chain.

Let us walk through a few more concrete examples from the remaining twenty-four stocks in XLP. Suppose a local restaurant in Texas orders weekly food supplies. There is a strong chance Sysco's refrigerated trucks deliver those boxes. Sysco is the largest foodservice distributor in XLP, linking farms and packers to millions of commercial kitchens.

Now picture a rural town miles away from any Costco warehouse. Families there often rely on Dollar General or Dollar Tree for quick fill-in trips—milk, paper towels, dish soap, and snacks. Those smaller-box discounters give XLP reach into lower-income and rural zip codes that warehouse clubs miss.

In the beverage aisle, XLP is not just cola. Monster Beverage brings high-margin energy drinks sold heavily in convenience stores. Keurig Dr Pepper combines single-serve coffee brewers with regional sodas. Constellation Brands imports Mexican beers like Modelo and Corona, adding a completely different growth curve.

In household and personal care, Kimberly-Clark supplies Huggies diapers and Kleenex tissues worldwide. Clorox owns bleach, trash bags, and Burt's Bees, while Church & Dwight owns Arm & Hammer baking soda and laundry pods. Together, they cover nearly every shelf in the cleaning and paper aisles.

Look at how those pieces fit together. When families cook at home more, Kroger, General Mills, and Clorox benefit. When they eat out more, Sysco and Coca-Cola's fountain business pick up the volume. That built-in balance is why XLP's aggregate revenue rarely swings wildly from year to year.

One final detail on XLP's top-ten weight: 64.28% in ten stocks sounds concentrated, yet those ten firms span all five major sub-industries. You get three retailers, two beverage giants, two household leaders, two tobacco firms, and one global snack maker. No single category dominates the entire ETF.

Let us pause on Target's role inside XLP, because many investors overlook it. Target runs over 1,900 stores and generated $106.57 billion in fiscal 2024 revenue. Inside that total, Food & Beverage brought in $23.83 billion and Household Essentials added $18.61 billion.

Combined, those everyday staples accounted for roughly 40% of Target's entire business. Add Target's owned brands and Drive Up curbside pickup, and you can see why GICS moved Target into Consumer Staples in 2023.

Consider Colgate-Palmolive's global reach as well. Roughly 84% of Colgate's 33,600 employees work outside the United States, across Asia Pacific, Latin America, and Europe. That global footprint lets Colgate capture rising middle-class oral care spending far beyond U.S. borders.

In the snacking aisle, Mondelez operates in over 150 countries with $38.54 billion in annual sales. Oreo biscuits, Ritz crackers, Cadbury chocolate, and Clif Bars give it unmatched impulse-snacking shelf space worldwide.

When you put all thirty-four companies together, XLP becomes a complete map of daily household habits. Morning coffee, toothpaste, laundry, lunch groceries, afternoon snacks, and evening retail runs all flow into one ticker.

Take a moment to appreciate how diverse XLP's revenue streams look at the checkout counter. A consumer might skip a new car or delay a home remodel during a slow economy. Yet that same household still buys toilet paper, baby diapers, coffee, and dish soap every week.

Look also at the pet-care anchor inside XLP. Colgate-Palmolive's Hill's Pet Nutrition and General Mills' Blue Buffalo tap into steady pet-ownership spending. Pet food behaves like a recurring subscription because owners rarely switch diets once a pet thrives on a formula.

That blend of human food, pet care, household cleaning, beverages, and retail distribution makes XLP far deeper than a simple grocery fund. Every aisle of the modern supercenter is represented inside its thirty-four holdings.
Think about the sheer daily reach of these thirty-four companies combined. On any given day in the United States, tens of millions of households swipe a card at Walmart, Costco, or Target.
Even more households open a bottle of Coca-Cola, brush with Crest or Colgate, or grab an Oreo cookie. XLP turns those routine daily habits into one unified equity position.
Put together, those six sub-industries give XLP balanced exposure across retail checkout counters, global beverage coolers, household cleaning aisles, and snack shelves.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION: The Margin Barbell Inside XLP
paragraphs: XLP is not a uniform basket. It is a barbell: 25.53% of the fund sits in three mega-retailers (Walmart, Costco, Target) earning 3.8% to 5.2% operating margins on massive inventory turns, while another 38.75% sits in seven brand and nicotine owners (P&G, Coca-Cola, PMI, Colgate, Altria, Mondelez, PepsiCo) earning 12% to 62% operating margins on intellectual property and distribution.
